Carnot efficiency is **1 − T₂/T₁** with both temperatures in **kelvin**.
**Step 1 — note that the temperatures are already absolute.**
T₁ = **500 K**, T₂ = **300 K** ✓ no conversion needed.
**Step 2 — substitute.**
η = 1 − 300/500
= 1 − 0·6
= **0·4** ✓
**Step 3 — express as a percentage.**
= **40%** ✓
**What this means in practice.** Of every 100 J absorbed from the source, **40 J**
becomes work and **60 J** is rejected to the sink ✓
**Why no engine can do better.** **Carnot's theorem**: no engine working between two
given temperatures can exceed the reversible efficiency ✓ A real engine, with friction
and finite-rate heat transfer, always falls short.
**How the efficiency could be raised.** Increase T₁ or decrease T₂ ✓ Raising the source
to 600 K would give 50%; lowering the sink to 200 K would give 60%. In practice the
sink is fixed by the environment, so engineers push the source temperature as high as
materials allow.
**Why 100% is impossible.** It would require T₂ = **0 K** ✓ unattainable by the third
law. Some heat must always be rejected - the Kelvin statement of the second law.
**The entropy check.** For a reversible cycle,
ΔS = −Q₁/T₁ + Q₂/T₂ = **0** ✓
With Q₁ = 100 J: Q₂ = 60 J, and −100/500 + 60/300 = −0·2 + 0·2 = 0 ✓ confirming
reversibility.
**The reversed cycle.** Run backwards it becomes a **refrigerator** with coefficient of
performance
T₂/(T₁ − T₂) = 300/200 = **1·5** ✓ moving 1·5 J of heat for each joule of work.
**Real efficiencies, for comparison.**
petrol engine: **25-30%**
diesel: **35-40%**
combined-cycle power station: **60%** ✓
each well below its own Carnot limit.
**Reading the distractors.** **60%** would be 1 − 200/500, and is not offered. **50%** ✗
needs T₂/T₁ = 0·5. **25%** ✗ needs 0·75, and **75%** ✗ needs 0·25 ✓ Only 300/500 = 0·6
gives 40%.
∴ 40%.

Water shows **anomalous expansion**: from 0 °C to 10 °C its volume **first decreases**,
then increases.
**Step 1 — follow the volume from 0 °C.** Heating water from 0 °C makes it
**contract** ✓ contrary to every intuition about thermal expansion.
**Step 2 — reach the turning point.** The contraction continues to **4 °C**, where the
volume is a **minimum** and the density a **maximum** ✓
**Step 3 — continue to 10 °C.** Beyond 4 °C the water behaves normally and
**expands** ✓
**Step 4 — conclude.** Over the range 0 °C to 10 °C the volume **first decreases and
then increases** ✓
**Why water behaves so oddly.** Below 4 °C the **hydrogen bonds** begin to lock the
molecules into the open, cage-like structure of ice ✓ That arrangement is less densely
packed than the liquid, so the volume grows as it forms.
**The density maximum.** **1000 kg m⁻³ at 4 °C** ✓ which is why the kilogram was
originally defined as the mass of a litre of water at that temperature.
**Why ice floats.** The same effect carried to completion ✓ Ice has a density of
**917 kg m⁻³**, some 9% less than water - a property almost unique, and one on which
life depends.
**The consequence for a freezing pond.** The surface water cools and sinks until the
whole body reaches 4 °C ✓ Further cooling makes the surface **lighter**, so it stays on
top, freezes, and insulates the water beneath. Fish survive the winter at 4 °C on the
bottom.
**What would happen otherwise.** Lakes would freeze **solid from the bottom up** ✓ and
most aquatic life in temperate regions would be impossible.
**How large the effect is.** Between 0 °C and 4 °C the density changes by only about
**0·013%** ✓ tiny, but enough to control the circulation of every lake on Earth.
**The practical nuisance.** Water expanding as it freezes **bursts pipes** and cracks
engine blocks ✓ and weathers rock by freeze-thaw action.
**Reading the distractors.** **Increases** ✗ describes the behaviour only above 4 °C.
**Decreases** ✗ only below it. **Does not change** ✗ would make water unique in another
way entirely ✓ Only the fourth option covers the whole range from 0 to 10 °C.
∴ first decreases and then increases.

Inside a charged shell the potential is **constant**; outside it falls as **1/r**.
**Step 1 — recall the two regimes.**
**inside or on** the shell (r ≤ R): V = **kq/R**, the same everywhere ✓
**outside** (r > R): V = **kq/r**, falling with distance ✓
**Step 2 — locate the three points.** The shell has radius **10 cm**:
5 cm: **inside** ✓
10 cm: **on the surface** ✓
15 cm: **outside** ✓
**Step 3 — compare.**
V₁ = kq/0·10 (inside, same as the surface)
V₂ = kq/0·10 (surface)
V₃ = kq/0·15 (outside) ✓
so
**V₁ = V₂ > V₃** ✓
**Why the potential is constant inside.** The **field** inside a charged conducting
shell is **zero** ✓ and
V(a) − V(b) = ∫E dr = 0
so no work is needed to move a charge about inside. The whole interior is at the
surface potential.
**Why it falls outside.** Beyond the shell the field is identical to that of a point
charge at the centre ✓ so the potential is kq/r, decreasing steadily to zero at
infinity.
**The numbers, with q chosen so that kq = 1 in these units.**
V₁ = V₂ = 1/0·10 = **10** ✓
V₃ = 1/0·15 = **6·67** ✓ two thirds of the surface value.
**The field, by contrast.**
inside: **zero** ✓
at the surface: kq/R², the maximum ✓
outside: kq/r², falling as the inverse square ✓
So the **field** jumps discontinuously at the surface, while the **potential** is
continuous - a general feature of surface charge distributions.
**Why the interior field is zero.** By **Gauss's law**, a sphere drawn inside the shell
encloses **no** charge ✓ so the flux, and with it the field, vanishes. This is the
principle of the **Faraday cage**.
**The practical consequence.** A sensitive instrument inside a metal enclosure is
shielded from external fields ✓ and a passenger inside a car is safe from lightning.
**Reading the distractors.** **V₁ > V₂ > V₃** ✗ supposes the potential keeps rising
inward - it does not. **V₁ < V₂ < V₃** ✗ reverses everything, and **V₁ = V₂ < V₃** ✗
has the potential rising with distance outside ✓
∴ V₁ = V₂ > V₃.

A pure inductor consumes **no average power** - the current is 90° out of phase with
the voltage.
**Step 1 — write the average power.**
P = V_rms I_rms **cos φ** ✓
**Step 2 — find the phase angle for a pure inductor.** The current **lags** the voltage
by exactly **90°** ✓ so
cos φ = cos 90° = **0** ✓
**Step 3 — conclude.**
**P = 0** ✓
**Where the energy goes instead.** It is **borrowed and repaid** each quarter-cycle ✓
During one quarter the inductor stores energy in its magnetic field, ½LI²; during the
next it returns it entirely to the source. Over a full cycle the net transfer is zero.
**The instantaneous power, which is not zero.**
p = VI sin ωt cos ωt = **(VI/2)sin 2ωt** ✓
oscillating at **twice** the supply frequency, positive for half of each cycle and
negative for the other half. Its average is zero.
**The term for this current.** **Wattless current** ✓ It flows, it heats the wires
through any resistance present, but it delivers no average power to the inductor
itself.
**Why this matters industrially.** Motors and transformers draw large reactive
currents ✓ The supply cables must carry them, losing energy as I²R, although no useful
power is delivered. Factories fit **capacitor banks** to cancel the inductive component
and raise the power factor towards 1.
**The contrast with a resistor.**
resistor: φ = 0, cos φ = 1, P = **VI** ✓ all the power consumed
inductor: φ = 90°, P = **0** ✓
capacitor: φ = −90°, P = **0** ✓
Only resistance dissipates energy.
**Why a real inductor does consume a little.** Its winding has **resistance**, and its
core suffers **hysteresis** and **eddy-current** losses ✓ so cos φ is small but not
exactly zero. The question specifies a **pure** inductor.
**The practical application.** A **choke** limits a.c. without dissipating power ✓
which is why fluorescent lamps used chokes rather than resistors - a resistor of the
same limiting effect would waste hundreds of watts as heat.
**Reading the distractors.** **½VI** ✗ is the peak of the instantaneous power, whose
**average** is zero. **VI²** ✗ and **VI²/4** ✗ are dimensionally wrong for a power ✓
∴ zero.

The **kinetic energies** follow from Einstein's equation, and the speeds go as their
square roots.
**Step 1 — find each maximum kinetic energy.**
KE = hν − φ ✓
first: 1 − 0·5 = **0·5 eV** ✓
second: 2·5 − 0·5 = **2·0 eV** ✓
**Step 2 — relate speed to energy.**
KE = ½mv², so **v ∝ √KE** ✓
**Step 3 — form the ratio.**
v₁/v₂ = √(0·5/2·0)
= √(1/4)
= **1/2** ✓
**Step 4 — state it.** **1 : 2** ✓
**Why the ratio is not 1 : 2·5.** The work function must be **subtracted first** ✓ The
photon energies are in the ratio 1 : 2·5, but the **useful** energies - what is left
after escaping the surface - are in the ratio 1 : 4. Taking the ratio of the photon
energies gives 1 : 1·58 and is the commonest error.
**Why the square root.** Energy goes as **v²** ✓ so a fourfold energy ratio gives only
a twofold speed ratio.
**The actual speeds.**
0·5 eV: v = √(2 x 0·5 x 1·6 x 10⁻¹⁹/9·1 x 10⁻³¹) = **4·2 x 10⁵ m s⁻¹** ✓
2·0 eV: **8·4 x 10⁵ m s⁻¹** ✓ exactly twice.
**Why both frequencies work.** Both photon energies exceed the work function of
0·5 eV ✓ Light of 0·4 eV, say, would eject **nothing**, however intense.
**The threshold frequency.**
ν₀ = φ/h = 0·5 x 1·6 x 10⁻¹⁹/6·63 x 10⁻³⁴ = **1·2 x 10¹⁴ Hz** ✓
corresponding to λ₀ = 1240/0·5 = **2480 nm**, in the infrared - a very low work
function, typical of caesium.
**What "maximum" speed means.** Electrons from the **surface** escape with the full
hν − φ ✓ Those from deeper down lose energy on the way out and emerge more slowly, so
there is a whole spread of speeds up to this maximum.
**How the stopping potentials would compare.**
eV₀ = KE_max, so V₀ = **0·5 V** and **2·0 V** ✓ in the ratio of the energies, 1 : 4 -
not of the speeds.
**Reading the distractors.** **1 : 5** ✗ and **1 : 4** ✗ are the energy ratios, not the
speed ratios. **1 : 1** ✗ would need equal kinetic energies ✓
∴ 1 : 2.

For uniform acceleration from rest, the **average** velocity is **half** the final
velocity.
**Step 1 — find the final velocity.**
v = u + gt
= 0 + 10(10)
= **100 m s⁻¹** ✓
**Step 2 — take the average.** With constant acceleration the velocity rises
**linearly**, so the mean is the mean of the endpoints:
v_av = (0 + 100)/2
= **50 m s⁻¹** ✓
**The check by distance over time.**
h = ½gt² = ½(10)(100) = **500 m** ✓
v_av = 500/10 = **50 m s⁻¹** ✓ the same, by the definition of average velocity.
**Why the two methods agree.** The **linearity** of v against t ✓ For a straight-line
graph, the mean value equals the midpoint value, and the area under it - the distance -
is the mean times the time.
**Why they would not agree for non-uniform acceleration.** With air resistance the
velocity curve bends ✓ and the simple endpoint average fails. One must then compute
distance ÷ time directly.
**A caution about average speed and average velocity.** Here they coincide, because the
motion is **in one direction** ✓ For a ball thrown up and caught again, the average
**velocity** over the whole flight is **zero** while the average **speed** is not.
**The velocity at the midpoint of the journey.** At h = 250 m:
v = √(2 x 10 x 250) = **70·7 m s⁻¹** ✓ not 50 - the body spends longer in the slow
early part, so the **time**-average is lower than the **distance**-midpoint value.
**The two averages contrasted.**
average over **time**: **50 m s⁻¹** ✓ what the question asks
velocity at the **mid-distance**: **70·7 m s⁻¹** ✓
A real and often-missed distinction.
**Is 10 s of free fall realistic?** It would mean a 500 m drop ✓ In air, a human reaches
terminal velocity of about 55 m s⁻¹ after some 12 s, so the ideal calculation
overestimates - but as an exercise in kinematics it is exact.
**Reading the distractors.** **100 m s⁻¹** ✗ is the **final** velocity, not the
average - the commonest slip. **10 m s⁻¹** ✗ is g read as a velocity, and **5 m s⁻¹** ✗
is half of that ✓
∴ 50 ms⁻¹.

Range goes as **sin 2θ**, and 30° and 60° are **complementary**, so they give equal
ranges - both less than 45°.
**Step 1 — write the range.**
R = **u² sin 2θ/g** ✓
With u the same for all three, only sin 2θ differs.
**Step 2 — evaluate it for each angle.**
30°: sin 60° = **0·866** ✓
45°: sin 90° = **1·000** ✓
60°: sin 120° = **0·866** ✓
**Step 3 — compare.**
**R_A = R_C < R_B** ✓
**Why 30° and 60° give the same range.** They are **complementary**: 30 + 60 = 90° ✓
and sin 2θ = sin(180° − 2θ), so sin 60° = sin 120°. Every pair of complementary angles
shares a range.
**Why 45° is the maximum.** sin 2θ peaks at 2θ = 90° ✓ which is the largest value the
sine can take, so R is greatest at θ = 45°.
**The numbers, for u = 20 m s⁻¹ and g = 10.**
30°: R = **34·6 m**, H = **5 m**, T = **2·0 s** ✓
45°: R = **40·0 m**, H = **10 m**, T = **2·83 s** ✓
60°: R = **34·6 m**, H = **15 m**, T = **3·46 s** ✓
Same range for the first and last, but very different **heights** and **flight times**.
**How the complementary pair differ.** The steeper launch gives a **higher** and
**longer** flight ✓ The shallower one is flatter and quicker. Which a gunner chooses
depends on whether he wants speed of arrival or a steep angle of descent.
**Why the maximum is so flat.** Near 45° the sine curve is at its peak and changes
slowly ✓ At 40° or 50° the range is still 98·5% of the maximum - which is why precision
in the launch angle matters less than one might expect.
**The caveat about air resistance.** With drag, the optimum falls to about **35°** ✓ and
the complementary symmetry is broken. The ideal result holds only in vacuum.
**A sanity check on the ordering.** The answer must put A and C **equal** - a
symmetry that no amount of arithmetic can disturb ✓ That alone eliminates two of the
four options.
**Reading the distractors.** **All equal** ✗ ignores the 45° maximum. **R_A = R_C >
R_B** ✗ inverts it, and **R_A < R_B < R_C** ✗ breaks the complementary symmetry ✓
∴ R_A = R_C < R_B.

The x component is **r cos θ**, which is greatest when **θ = 0** - the vector lying
along the positive x-axis.
**Step 1 — write the component.**
r_x = **r cos θ** ✓
with θ measured from the x-axis.
**Step 2 — maximise it.** cos θ reaches its greatest value, **+1**, at **θ = 0** ✓ so
r_x = **r**, the whole magnitude.
**Step 3 — conclude.** The component is maximum when **r̄ is along the positive
x-axis** ✓
**The values at the other options.**
along **+y** (θ = 90°): cos 90° = 0, so r_x = **0** ✓
along **−y** (θ = 270°): again **0** ✓
at **45°**: cos 45° = 0·707, so r_x = **0·707r** ✓ substantial, but not maximum.
**Why a component can never exceed the magnitude.** cos θ is bounded by 1 ✓ so
|r_x| ≤ r always - a useful check on any resolution.
**The minimum.** At θ = 180°, cos θ = **−1** and r_x = **−r** ✓ maximum in magnitude
but **negative** - pointing along −x. The question asks for the maximum **value**, so
+r at θ = 0 is the answer.
**Why components matter.** They let a vector problem be split into **independent**
one-dimensional problems along each axis ✓ Projectile motion, equilibrium of forces and
circuit analysis all depend on it.
**The two components together.**
r_x = r cos θ, r_y = r sin θ ✓
and r_x² + r_y² = r²(cos²θ + sin²θ) = **r²** ✓ Pythagoras, as it must be - so when one
component is maximum the other is necessarily **zero**.
**The direction recovered.** θ = tan⁻¹(r_y/r_x) ✓ so a vector with zero y component
lies exactly along x.
**A practical instance.** Pulling a sledge with a rope ✓ The useful horizontal force is
F cos θ, greatest when the rope is **horizontal**. Pulling at 45° wastes 29% of the
effort lifting rather than hauling.
**Why the angle is measured from x.** It is the convention when the x component is
wanted ✓ Measuring from the y-axis would swap the roles of sine and cosine - the
commonest source of confusion in resolution problems.
**Reading the distractors.** **Along +y** and **along −y** ✗ both give zero x
component. **At 45°** ✗ gives 0·707r, large but not the maximum ✓
∴ r̄ is along + ve x − axis.
